item.title: The Guitar.com Magazine September/October 2026 issue with Towa Bird on the cover is now on sale
item.dc:creator: Guitar.com
item.description:
Plus a copy of NME Magazine, featuring Akriila on the cover.

The post The Guitar.com Magazine September/October 2026 issue with Towa Bird on the cover is now on sale appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
item.content:encoded:
The September/October 2026 issue of Guitar.com Magazine, with Towa Bird on the cover, is out now – alongside a copy of NME Magazine featuring Chilean rapper/singer Akriila.

Following Mateus Asato, Yvette Young, Jacob Collier and Grace Bowers, Towa Bird is our latest print cover star. Don’t wait – grab your bundle of Guitar.com and NME Magazine now via Dawsons.

Speaking to Z. Raza-Sheikh, Towa Bird reflects on going back to her guitar roots in her current era, anchored by her latest album Gentleman, collaborating with Kathleen Hanna, and how she’s writing new music from a place of “a place of security and joy, rather than desperation and approval seeking”. Read the digital cover story now, which features photography by Kristen Jan Wong.

Also in the new issue: our deep-diving feature with Tosin Abasi on the Abasi Stage 7; a close-up exploration of Kirk Hammett’s ESP KH-2 Ouija; interviews with The Linda Lindas and Zoh Amba, and much more.

Want to be first in line next time? Subscribe here for more information about Guitar.com Magazine and for the chance to receive an exclusive queue jump opportunity, where readers can get their hands on a copy before anyone else. Guitar.com sends out queue jump tickets shortly before the magazine goes on sale to mailing list subscribers.

item.title: “I thought it went better with the guitar!”: Johnny Marr reveals he chose his famous hairstyle to compliment this specific guitar
item.dc:creator: Sam Roche
item.description:
The guitarist recalls the first time he rocked up to a photo session with his new look: “The rest of the band were like, ‘What have you done?’”

The post “I thought it went better with the guitar!”: Johnny Marr reveals he chose his famous hairstyle to compliment this specific guitar appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
item.content:encoded:
Johnny Marr is known for his distinctive look as much as his guitar playing in The Smiths and as a solo artist, but it was no accident.

As he explains in a new interview with LIFEJACKET on YouTube, the Mancunian legend recalls how his distinctive mod-crop hairstyle was inspired by the “Beatle who never made it”, Stuart Sutcliffe, and how he chose his look to complement a specific guitar in his arsenal. 

That guitar was, of course, his famous Jetglo-finished 1982 Rickenbacker 330, bought at a Manchester guitar shop in ‘83 and used extensively across the Smiths’ self-titled debut album and on tour.

“One of my heroes at the time was Stuart Sutcliffe,” he recalls. “I thought, ‘I really wanna look like Stu Sutcliffe.’ V-neck jumper, white polo neck, Ray-Bans. The shop I worked in, we were the first ones to sell the Wayfarers when they came back. So, I was like, ‘I’m having those.’

  • READ MORE: Johnny Marr reacts to Andy Burnham playing the Smiths with Ukrainian soldiers: “It’s a victory for the guitar”

He continues: “The Smiths had the quiffs, the ‘ 50s thing. But because I was into Stu Sutcliffe, he combed his hair down and did the Beatle cut. So that’s where that came from. He looked even better when he combed his hair down.”

Marr remembers the first time he showed up to a Smiths photo shoot rocking his new look. “The rest of the band were like, ‘What have you done?’ I just rocked up and I had the bowl cut then. I thought it went better with the guitar. 

“I knew I was gonna get a Rickenbacker, so the bowl thing and the Rickenbacker. All of these obsessive little details came into play.”

Everyone’s influenced by someone, of course, and the Smiths quickly noticed following their rapid success that their fans were beginning to adopt their look themselves.

“The fans all dressed like different members of the band, which is kinda cool,” Marr continues. “So when you rocked up at Bangor University or Loughborough or somewhere like that, there’d be a bunch of kids outside, and you’d be like, ‘Okay, there’s Andy, there’s Johnny.’

“We’d look out the window of the bus and there’d be these kids dressed like us. And because we were kids ourselves, it’s kind of a bit of a buzz up there. Because you’re building a culture. You’re missing a trick if you think a band is just about the music. If you look at Fontaines D.C. now, they’ve got such a strong look. You’re always drawing from someone, it’s never entirely original.”

Marr’s ‘82 Jetglo Rickenbacker 330 found a new home last month, selling for a respectable £358,400 during a Christie’s auction which saw the Smiths guitarist sell off a bunch of guitars and other items from his personal collection.

The auction – which took place on 17 September and brought in £3,649,280 in total – also saw the sale of Marr’s Cherry Red 1960 Gibson ES-355, which sold for over £200,000, and the 1971 Martin D-28 acoustic used on Rusholme Ruffians, What She Said and Meat is Murder, which brought in £128,000.

The post “I thought it went better with the guitar!”: Johnny Marr reveals he chose his famous hairstyle to compliment this specific guitar appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.

item.title: Five reasons why you need to try the new Spark Pedal
item.dc:creator: Josh Gardner
item.description:
Positive Grid’s latest iteration on its brilliant smart amp brings it to the floor – and makes it more versatile than ever.

The post Five reasons why you need to try the new Spark Pedal appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
item.content:encoded:
Ad feature with Positive Grid

Positive Grid’s Spark smart amp has been one of the most revolutionary new guitar products of the last decade. With its great sound and ease of use, it has completely changed what people expect from home practice amps, while the range has expanded to ensure that no matter what musical situation you might find yourself in, the Spark can help you sound great with minimal fuss. 

The latest addition to the range is the Spark Pedal, and it might be the most versatile and useful Spark product yet. With its compact pedal-based form factor, it has the potential to be a wonderfully useful bridge between home, stage and studio. These are our top five reasons why you need to give the Spark Pedal a try next time you’re in a guitar store. 

Its sounds and usability are as good as ever

The reason that so many guitar players have been charmed by the Spark ecosystem is how remarkably easy it is to build your own sounds, with rugged and clear multifunction knobs that make it easy to dial in sounds in a heartbeat. 

But that’s only part of it – the benchmark-setting companion smartphone app that controls all of the complicated stuff, you can easily build your signal chain in moments, hearing them in real time on the device. And what good sounds they are too – with 33 high-quality amp models and 43 effects using the same HD Tone engine as the Spark 2, you can run the gamut of all the classic amps and effects you’d ever need – and they all sound remarkably faithful and organic, whether running through a PA or headphones. 

It’s truly a Spark for any situation

While the original Spark was designed for relatively quiet home practice and recording, the various other models in the range have expanded the offering to cover any scenario – from full-on live performances and busking to bedroom headphone jamming. The Spark Pedal however, manages to be everything in one. 

Of course, if you want to play at home, you can either plug into the headphone jack and enjoy impressive sounds in cans, or you can run it into your PC speakers or a powered cab. If you’re recording? Well the built-in USB-C recording interface makes going direct a doddle, but there’s more. For gigging guitarists, the Spark Pedal might be the most versatile box yet – you can choose to run it direct into a powered cab or PA live, or you could bypass the amp models and use the onboard effects going into a traditional amp. Indeed, the Spark Pedal plays nicely at the end of your existing pedalboard, with stereo outs, an expression pedal jack, and even MIDI control to ensure that you can program any element of your performance to go off without a hitch. 

And with a built-in 60-second looper, the Spark Pedal is the perfect companion for solo guitarists looking to build their song from the ground up. And with simple and easy to understand controls for the looper built right into the Pedal’s three footswitches, you won’t have any trouble when it comes to overdubs and syncing your playing up just right. 

You don’t have to worry about powering it

If you’re trying to run light at a gig, or you’re performing at a location where plentiful supplies of power sockets are not forthcoming (and we’ve all been there) the Spark Pedal takes the stress out of your set-up. With its built-in rechargeable battery that offers up to 7 hours of playing time, you don’t need to fumble around looking for a power outlet – simply turn it on, plug it in, and you’re ready to rock. 

You can find your tone in a heartbeat

One of the most exciting features about the whole Spark ecosystem is how easy and fun it is to find the tone you’re looking for. Thanks to the busy folks on Positive Grid’s ToneCloud platform, there are now over 100,000 different user-created presets that you can search through, often ones aimed at nailing the tone of a specific song or artist. If you’re playing covers, this is an absolute godsend, and means that you can be as flexible in your set as your songbook allows. In addition to the onboard presets, if you don’t want to use something someone else has made, Spark AI’s Text to Tone feature lets the computer do the hard work, building a totally new tone from your prompt. 

It’s built for the road

The build quality and smart physical design of the Spark amps has always been a huge strength, and the Spark Pedal takes this and makes it even more useful. With its compact form factor, you can easily fit it in the pocket of a gigbag, but with a metal chassis and rugged metal footswitches, you don’t have to worry about it getting damaged. What’s more, a rubbery neoprene shell and rubber feet mean that you don’t have to worry about it moving around on stage too much either. 

Another reassuring thing about the Spark Pedal’s design is its stripped down control layout. There’s no LCD screen to worry about treading on here – with the deep editing done via the app, what’s on the pedal is designed for those moments where you need to make quick changes on the fly, and you can do those without worrying about how it’s going to mess up your sound if you get it wrong. 

With versatility, connectivity, portability and durability the Spark Pedal would be great anyway, but add all that to the great tones and ease of use that we’re already used to from Positive Grid, and you have a gigging guitarist’s new best friend.

Find out more about the Spark Pedal at Positive Grid. 

 

The post Five reasons why you need to try the new Spark Pedal appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.

item.title: “You saw heavy metal bands doing power ballads!”: Why MTV nearly made Steve Morse quit music for a VERY different career
item.dc:creator: Sam Roche
item.description:
“These platforms were ruling the musical decisions that were happening,” says the guitarist.

The post “You saw heavy metal bands doing power ballads!”: Why MTV nearly made Steve Morse quit music for a VERY different career appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
item.content:encoded:
With his work alongside some of rock’s most notable legacy acts including Deep Purple, Kansas and Dixie Dregs, Steve Morse has been instrumental in shaping the world of rock music and guitar as we know it today. His career has exclusively been in music, though. For a brief period in the late ‘80s, the guitarist served as a regional airline pilot.

A longtime pilot and aviation enthusiast, Morse started flying as a teenager, and bought his first plane for about $4,000 while attending the University of Miami in the ‘70s. And his passion for flying ultimately led to a six-month stint as an airline pilot. But what prompted such a radical career shift amid a hugely successful music career?

  • READ MORE: “The jazz people were laughing when they saw me at the audition with my Telecaster”: Steve Morse reflects on his early guitar journey

As the 72-year-old guitarist explains to Guitar World’s Matt Owen in a new interview, it came down to a disillusionment with the music industry and the increasing demand from record labels and management for music to have MTV and mainstream TV appeal.

“[MTV] had developed into this thing. I was in the band Kansas, and I was like, ‘I’m gonna write a bunch of cool instrumental stuff like Kerry Livgren did… I thought that was gonna be what we were doing.

“But there was a big push from management and the record company: ‘We need a hit single that could play on VH1 or MTV.’ And so these platforms were kind of ruling the musical decisions that were happening. And it was happening everywhere. You saw heavy metal bands doing power ballads just to have a video on VH1.

“And I was just at the point in my life where I said, ‘You know what, I knew the music business would change. I didn’t know what it would change to.”

Morse ultimately left Kansas in the late ‘80s to work on his own music. “I’m gonna record whatever I wanna record,” he remembers thinking to himself. “So it just became, ‘I’m gonna work on my own music. I don’t care what it is. I ended up writing some of the best stuff I ever did for High Tension Wires [his 1989 solo album], because I just didn’t care anymore.”

“It’s not that I didn’t care about the music, I just didn’t care about whether the record company or the manager liked it or not. I just said, ‘I know some people will like this, and I will find where those people go and play gigs where they are.’ It was very liberating.”

It was during this stint as a solo artist that Morse decided to obtain his licence to be a commercial pilot. He ultimately qualified and worked as a pilot for an Atlanta-based regional airline for six months, but notes his short time in the position was down to it being a “really bad time to be a pilot”.

“They had so many pilots applying for the positions that they could do anything they wanted, and they did,” he remembers.

“They didn’t pay us anything to start with, so I was broke. I was booking gigs on my days off. I had to work Christmas Eve, Christmas, New Year’s Ever and New Years. And on the days in between I booked a solo gig so I could make enough money to keep the electricity on in my trailer.”

Morse ended up in a face-off with his bosses: “They drafted me, and said, ‘You have to come into work.’ I said, ‘I can’t, I have a gig.’ They said, ‘You have to.’ I said, ‘I can’t.’ They said, ‘Well you’re gonna have to quit.’ And I did.”

The decision to quit being a commercial pilot was influenced, however, after he received an invitation to perform with Lynyrd Skynyrd.

“Gary Rossington had called me up right before that and invited me down to the Omni [venue in Atlanta, Georgia]. He was getting back together with Lynyrd Skynyrd… He said, ‘Morse, bring your guitar.’ And I get down there, they’re already on stage. The crew says, ‘Alright, go up now.’ And they said, ‘Alright we’re bringing out special guest Steve Morse!’”

item.title: Lloyd Baggs on developing a revolutionary new acoustic pickup with Gibson, and why it’s the fulfillment of a lifetime of searching for better acoustic sound
item.dc:creator: Eric Dahl
item.description:
The legendary acoustic pickup maker has teamed up with Gibson to launch the new HiFi DNA pickup – he tells us why its a fitting way to celebrate four decades of redefining acoustic amplification

The post Lloyd Baggs on developing a revolutionary new acoustic pickup with Gibson, and why it’s the fulfillment of a lifetime of searching for better acoustic sound appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
item.content:encoded:
There are few individuals who can definitively say that they have redefined the guitar industry, but Lloyd Baggs is one of them. Baggs has played a huge part in the evolution of amplified acoustic guitar sound over the last four decades. In fact, you can make a very strong case that, were it not for the innovation that Baggs and his counterpart Larry Fishman a few years earlier brought to the industry, the state of our live acoustic guitar sound might be a horribly unsatisfactory one.

  • READ MORE: LR Baggs AEG-1 – is this the new best-sounding electro-acoustic on the market?

Since Baggs first transitioned from making carbon fibre guitars to designing his first pickup in his California garage in the mid-80s, Baggs has been on a quest to improve the sound we hear when we plug in an acoustic – whether that’s via the pickup, preamp, all the way through to building a game-changing instrument of his own, the AEG-1 in 2024.

Things are changing at LR Baggs, however. Earlier this month, the company announced that it would drop Lloyd’s initials from the company name and just be known as “Baggs” going forward. And then came the announcement of a partnership with Gibson on the new HiFi DNA pickup system that the man himself described as “a big leap forward” for acoustic pickups. So, what’s going on…?

First up, why did you decide to change the company name after such a long time?

“That’s some news! We just rolled out our new website, and it is LR free, except for the history and friendships. It’s Baggs moving forward mostly to honor the team. Our daughter joining the company as creative director is huge. She’s been working on this for about a year to really tell the story of who we are.”

Most companies would be nervous about changing their name with such a long legacy and brand value…

“The change in name is not a change in philosophy. I think it’s more externalising the philosophy that the Baggs company already had. Jenny [Lloyd’s daughter] is just telling our story better. And the last thing I ever wanted us to be doing is relaunching and rebranding. It’s like, the three Rs brand management are: rebrand, relaunch, and resign! [laughs]. It’s funny, a lot of people have been calling us Baggs forever and we started it when we brought out the AEG guitars. We’ve been wanting to do this for about 10 years.”

The partnership with Gibson is a really exciting one, how did that all come about?

“Well, Gibson is our longest abiding vendor. They’ve been with us longer than any other OEM customer we’ve ever had. We started back in ‘87 with the just steel-string, and we just kind of rolled it forward through all the various iterations of the company.

“They became our biggest customers during the Henry [Juszkiewicz, Gibson CEO until 2019] years. And with the new administration, Cesar really opened it up and empowered the great people at Gibson. So, fast-forward to today and Cesar was giving us credit for being in their guitars and talking about it. I guess about three years or so ago, we introduced the first HiFis.

“It took Gibson a while to figure out how good the original HiFis was, and they started loving it, and their artists were asking for them. It made its way onto some models, and Cesar [Gueikian, former Gibson CEO and current board member] fell in love with it. And I asked Gibson if they would have any interest in expanding our business relationship with the HiFis on an exclusive level. But unfortunately, the horse was already out of the barn and, and several other Gibson competitors were already adopting the HiFi on their guitars. So, Gibson threw it back over the fence and said, ‘Well, how’d you like to create something for us that we could have on our own for a while and it might even be better?’”

When the original HiFi pickups were launched, there was a real buzz around the industry because of both the design of it, but also sounds and the affordability of the system, but this is something a little different right?

“Well it’s still a bridgeplate transducer, and let me back up here a tiny bit into what a bridgeplate transducer offers. Placing a transducer on the bridgeplate puts it further from the strings and from the saddle. It’s got more body in it, and it just sounds better to me. Plus the bridgeplate’s just a nicer place to pick up energy from than right directly underneath the string.

“There have been many bridgeplate pickups in the market over the years, of course. Some of them were more successful than others, but some were really feedback prone. But this new HiFi DNA is something brand new.”

How so?

“It’s got an upgraded, lighter, more flexible transducer, and it’s more sensitive. The first thing we wanted to see was if we could improve the sound of the pickups themselves. And I believe we’ve made a big improvement there. The sensor is 25 per cent of the mass and about 20 per cent of the thickness of the original sensor.

“But I think the most significant part that really puts it over the top is that the original HiFi sensor A and sensor B are summed together and then sent into the preamp. Now think about two nice big mic diaphragms sitting next to each other for a vocalist, you’re recording in stereo, only instead of each mic diaphragm having its own preamp, you wire them together and you put them into one preamp.

“The HiFi DNA system treats it as though each microphone diaphragm has its own preamp built into the microphone. We created an individual, all discrete, class A, studio quality preamp for each pickup, and we voiced it for that specific location.

“They don’t share an EQ; they’re not quite the same in gain. Basically, each one is doing its job maintaining the purity of the signal from that voice on that side of the guitar versus the other. Each preamp is maintaining the purity of each signal and conditioning each signal to be more ideal before they’re summed together actively after the preamps. You’re able to mix those independently instead of as the original HiFi where both were summed into one.”

And this is going to roll out to the whole Gibson range?

“They’re putting them in a lot of guitars right now – the Hummingbird, Dove and J-45 from the Modern Collection, and the SJ-200, Songwriter, L-00 and LG-2 in the Original Collection. It’s going to be a Gibson exclusive for three years.”

Hearing it in action, it seems to offer a very natural sound without the muddy bass or high-end brittleness that acoustic pickups can deliver.

“I believe this is the best thing that we have ever done, and what I’ve been trying to do since my experience of Ry Cooder swearing at his rack in the early days. Those were painful days of acoustic amplification, and the goal was to make the process of playing an acoustic guitar rewarding and enjoyable. It’s been our career goal to make that a reality. And I believe that the HiFi DNA is the closest that we have come to that goal.”

The LR Baggs HiFi DNA pickup system is available exclusively from Gibson, and can be bought as an upgrade kit for $299. Find out more at gibson.com.

The post Lloyd Baggs on developing a revolutionary new acoustic pickup with Gibson, and why it’s the fulfillment of a lifetime of searching for better acoustic sound appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.

item.title: Unlock the crucial wah tone of Iron Maiden’s Killers album with this discounted signature Cry Baby pedal
item.dc:creator: Rachel Roberts
item.description:
The pedal was launched earlier this year for NAMM, and was even gifted to Kirk Hammett.

The post Unlock the crucial wah tone of Iron Maiden’s Killers album with this discounted signature Cry Baby pedal appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
item.content:encoded:
Calling all Iron Maiden fans – you can now get your hands on the signature Iron Maiden x Dunlop Cry Baby wah pedal that launched earlier this year at The NAMM Show for less.

Now reduced to £169 at Thomann as part of its Guitar Day deals for a limited time only, fans and collectors alike can own the crucial wah tone used across the band’s landmark Killers album from 1981, which is certified Gold in both the US and UK.

  • READ MORE: The best picks for electric guitar and acoustic guitar, from Jim Dunlop, Fender, Ibanez and more

The pedal has a rather cool design on its face, featuring none other than the band’s skeletal mascot, Eddie, taken right from the Killers album artwork. It also features the Killers title in the same font it appears in on the album’s cover, while the band’s logo runs along the side of the unit.

At the time of its release earlier this year, Metallica’s Kirk Hammett was one of the first artists to get his hands on the pedal. He shared a video to Instagram opening the pedal, in which you can also get a glimpse of its packaging – also worthy of display.

View this post on Instagram

Beneath its Iron Maiden design and fittingly metal exterior, the pedal itself is essentially the classic GCB95 Cry Baby Standard Wah. Find out more and get a better look in the short video below:

Iron Maiden were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame this year, five whole decades after their debut. But interestingly, the band haven’t felt like making much of a fuss about it.

Speaking to Metal Hammer in June, bassist Steve Harris and frontman Bruce Dickinson made it clear that while they’re grateful for the recognition, it’s never been something they’ve spent much time thinking about.

Harris said, “It’s never really bothered me one way or the other, because awards aren’t what we do this for. But in a weird way I’m glad it’s happened so the Americans will stop banging on about it. To me, if you get offered something, you say, ‘Thank you very much.’ But did I lose sleep over getting it or not getting it? No.”

Shop the Iron Maiden CryBaby pedal at Thomann now.

The post Unlock the crucial wah tone of Iron Maiden’s Killers album with this discounted signature Cry Baby pedal appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.

item.title: “I’m going to play in front of how many? 40,000?!”: America’s Got Talent winner Nene Royal on being invited to open for Avenged Sevenfold
item.dc:creator: Sam Roche
item.description:
The 16-year-old star details how she landed the support slot for A7X’s upcoming show in Singapore.

The post “I’m going to play in front of how many? 40,000?!”: America’s Got Talent winner Nene Royal on being invited to open for Avenged Sevenfold appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
item.content:encoded:
It’s the stuff dreams are made of. Just months ago, 16-year-old Rattikarn Amloy was a relatively unknown guitar player. But following an audition on the 2026 season of America’s Got Talent – during which she performed a blistering cover of Cranberries classic Zombie – her life changed forever.

Performing as Nene Royal, the guitar sensation – who originally hails from Phuket, Thailand – stormed her way through the competition, dazzling audiences and the nation with covers of Soundgarden’s Black Hole Sun, The White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army and Muse’s Hysteria, and even joining Linkin Park themselves for a performance of their track The Emptiness Machine, before going on to win the entire show last week.

Yep, Amloy is just 16 years of age and she’s already achieved success most musicians only dream of. But she’s just getting started. In fact, her whirlwind story continues, as she’s been invited to open for one of metal’s biggest bands, Avenged Sevenfold, for their upcoming Singapore show on 13 October.

  • READ MORE: Guitar legend John Mayer is playing six nights at the Las Vegas Sphere – here’s everything you need to know

In the past few months, she’s gained considerable experience performing to large audiences – not to mention millions viewing from home. But opening for A7X, one of her favourite bands? The pressure’s on…

View this post on Instagram

Speaking to Metal Hammer in a new interview, the guitarist explains how she landed the gig to open for Avenged. “The managers in Singapore text me: ‘Oh, I hear you wanna play with Avenged Sevenfold?’” she recalls.

“I was like, ‘Yeah!’ They said, ‘Well, Avenged Sevenfold want you to support them.’ They asked for me, ‘Do you wanna do it?’ And I was like, ‘Yeah!’”

As for her feelings in the runup to the show, she confesses she’s both excited and scared in equal measure.

“It’s my first time playing support to Avenged Sevenfold, so I was like, ‘I’m scared!’ And I’m going to play in front of how many? 40,000!”

Elsewhere in the interview, the Royal reveals she had no idea she was going to perform with Linkin Park before doing so during the AGT final. “I was practising on my own. I thought I was going to play alone,” she says. “But when I practised, a cameraman just came in, and then Linkin Park came in. I was like, ‘What’s going on?!’ I don’t know if Linkin Park are just gonna come and take a video, some shot, that’s all. But actually, [they] say, ‘We’re gonna join together onstage,’ and I was like, ‘There’s no way!’ My dream’s come true.”

You can catch Nene Royal opening for Avenged Sevenfold on 13 October at the Singapore Indoor Stadium. Tickets are available via the Avenged Sevenfold website.

The post “I’m going to play in front of how many? 40,000?!”: America’s Got Talent winner Nene Royal on being invited to open for Avenged Sevenfold appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.

item.title: John Mayer thinks big guitar makers have “punished” affordable guitars by making them look worse than expensive ones
item.dc:creator: Sam Roche
item.description:
Do guitar companies save the more aesthetically pleasing colourways for their more expensive lines?

The post John Mayer thinks big guitar makers have “punished” affordable guitars by making them look worse than expensive ones appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
item.content:encoded:
One of the coolest guitar releases of the year so far – hell, in recent memory – was the spate of limited-edition PRS Silver Skys outfitted in classic Land Rover Defender colourways launched last earlier this month.

It marked the announcement of an unexpected partnership between the guitar maker and Jaguar Land Rover, driven chiefly by the Silver Sky’s namesake John Mayer’s love of the legendary SUV. 

The collab consists of eight Silver Sky models boasting Defender finishes: four USA-made ones sporting classic Defender colourways like Arles Blue and Sandglow Yellow, and four SE models wearing some more contemporary finishes, like Petra Copper and Woolstone Green.

And a big part of the collaboration for Mayer was ensuring those with more SE-adjacent budgets weren’t being shortchanged in terms of the look of the guitars in comparison to the more expensive USA-made models.

  • READ MORE: Guitar legend John Mayer is playing six nights at the Las Vegas Sphere – here’s everything you need to know

In a new interview with Guitar World following the launch, the guitar maestro – who has also just announced a huge six-night residency at the Las Vegas Sphere, his second stint at the venue after a lengthy residency with Dead & Company in 2024 and 2025 – explains why it was important to make sure the more budget-friendly Silver Sky Defenders also looked the part.

Notably, the SE models – which despite their limited run are priced at a reasonable £799 apiece – are the first Silver Skys to feature a highly requested black pickguard.

“It’s almost like the first appearance of Wolverine. Everyone’s waiting for it,” Mayer says. “I think it’s interesting that it makes its appearance on the SE line as opposed to just having it trickle down from the Core line.”

“I thought it was nice to give something to the SE,” he continues. “When I was growing up, the more accessible guitar got punished for being more accessible. I learned a lot from the SE.

“I originally had the idea like, ‘Oh, you tier it.’ Then guitar lovers of the world spoke to me. I learned that some people are going to have an SE forever. It doesn’t have to be a consolation and someday you’ll work your way up. That’s when I thought, ‘There should be a little bit to separate the lines.’”

It is, indeed, common for guitar companies to separate colourway options for their differently priced guitar lines, and some argue that the more aesthetically pleasing colours tend to be available on more expensive models. But that was the opposite of Mayer’s approach to the Defender collaboration.

“Teaming up with Defender to offer the Silver Sky guitar in their legendary 4×4 colors is a dream come true,” said Mayer, a keen Defender enthusiast, when the collab was announced. 

“I’ve always chosen colourways based on objects and materials that inspire me in the world, and as a collector and lover of Defenders, this collaboration is the perfect crossover between two great passions of mine.”

Learn more about the new limited-edition Silver Sky Defender guitars at PRS.

item.title: Martin D-X2E Molly Tuttle review: “if I closed my eyes, I really could tell myself I was playing a 1940s guitar”
item.dc:creator: Eric Dahl
item.description:
The Mexico-made affordable version of Molly Tuttle’s signature model is the most expensive X Series guitar yet – is it worth the extra investment?

The post Martin D-X2E Molly Tuttle review: “if I closed my eyes, I really could tell myself I was playing a 1940s guitar” appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
item.content:encoded:
$999/£999, martinguitar.com

The world of bluegrass flat-picking acoustic guitar is in rude health at the moment, as a new generation is elevating and propagating the form to new audiences and new levels – from Billy Strings and Trey Hensley, to Chris Eldridge and Cody Kilby, and many others.

  • READ MORE: Martin Road Series DC-13E Modern review: a stunning cutaway Dreadnought aimed at contemporary players

And then there’s Molly Tuttle. The 33-year-old Californian is a two-time IBMA guitar player of the year and back-to-back winner of the Grammy Award for Best Bluegrass Album, and was even nominated in its hugely prestigious Best New Artist category in 2023. That’s an honour shared in recent years by everyone from Noah Kahan and Gracie Abrams, to Ice Spice and Chappell Roan.

All of which to say is that Tuttle is not just a flatpicking guitarist of rare talent, but one whose artistry is crossing the floor to bring a whole new audience into the realm of bluegrass and Americana.

As is usually the case with flatpickers, Tuttle has been a great exponent of the Martin dreadnought throughout her career, and so it makes all the sense in the world that Martin would honour her not just with one signature model, but two. There’s a fancy Nazareth-made D-18 for the well-heeled ($4,199.99), but interestingly also a more affordable Mexico-made version, we’re looking at the latter.

What is it?

The DX-2E Molly Tuttle is, like its US-made sibling, inspired by Tuttle’s most beloved and cherished Martin: a 1943 D-18. The most notable thing that sets it apart from a regular X Series dreadnought is the neck profile, which is a fast, comfortable 1940s carve with the same 1 11/16″ nut width. This 1941 carve has a soft V to it, and unlike most of the X Series guitars, it has a standard taper, so it doesn’t get narrower as you move up the neck.

The other striking differences are mainly cosmetic – the spruce top is finished with a lovely vintage sunburst, while the satin-finished HPL back and sides have a vintage mahogany pattern. The ebony fingerboard features a faux abalone and pearl custom Moon Phase pattern on it, and you also get a silver logo on the headstock, plus a set of open-gear tuners with custom oval buttons.

Otherwise, it’s pretty much the same as a standard Martin DX-2E – with a solid top, HPL back and sides, a select hardwood neck, and Martin E-1 electronics. You also get a plush Martin-branded gig bag.

Build and playability

Upon pulling the guitar out of the aforementioned gig bag, the aesthetics of Tuttle’s DX-2E really grabbed my attention. The satin-finished top with its vintage sunburst gives a very ‘old’ vibe, and sat on a guitar stand across from my desk, it really does look like a pre-war Martin, at first glance at least. The more rounded shape of the headstock compared to a modern Martin, combined with those open-gear tuners, really does change the vibe of the guitar and make it seem more classic and worn in – a nice touch.

Picking it up, and on close inspection I’m less taken with the lack of binding – a feature common to all X Series but one that really does make the guitar feel less premium. I understand that there are likely cost and range-differentiation reasons behind this (the Road Series exists after all!) but on a signature model like this, especially one that costs $200 more than a regular DX-2E, it’s a shame to have the illusion broken so easily.

Because when you play the thing, it’s very easy to forget that you are in fact playing an X Series, because this satin-finished 1941 neck is an absolute superstar. I’ve played a few pre-war Martins, and you can tell the care and attention that’s gone into getting this profile and feel just right. When I closed my eyes, I really could tell myself I was playing a 1940s guitar.

What’s more, in contrast to say, the slimmer nut of the Billy Strings model that seemed more readily designed for bluegrass picking at speed, the fingerboard here feels like a nice, accommodating middle ground that will suit any playing style. It’s something that the original 40s Martin dreadnoughts did so well, and it’s very impressive that the company has recreated it here.

Sounds

It might be damning the DX-2E with faint praise to say that it sounds like a standard Martin dreadnought, but in truth that’s exactly what it’s supposed to be. It’s absolutely not going to trick my ears into thinking that it’s a 1940s guitar in the way it fooled my eyes and hands, but this is a sub-$1,000 guitar we’re dealing with here, c’mon!

What it offers is a powerful, strident voice that’s warm and subtle, and I do notice a bit more treble and mid-frequency bite than a typical Martin dread, which is all rather pleasant.

Plugged into an amplifier, I found the E-1 system to be very usable and effective – it does a nice job of replicating the unplugged sound. The subtle soundhole controls are really handy in the heat of battle, as is the onboard tuner, which looks up at you from inside the bottom of the soundhole. Some may not love what it does to the aesthetics of the guitar, but I like how the E-1 system’s battery is stowed behind a flip-up plastic cover around the strap button – it’s a lot easier than fishing around the guitar for a velcro’d battery inside!

Should I buy one?

This is another really impressive Mexico-made signature model from Martin – the Navojoa team is doing some really fantastic work right now, and we’re seeing the best of it in how they’re being entrusted with artist guitars like these.

The great thing about this guitar in particular is how much of a great all-rounder it is – that neck is one of the finest Martin carves I’ve felt outside of the Nazareth factory, and you can tell it’s put a lot of time and effort into nailing the playability and feel of Tuttle’s guitar.

It’s a shame that the aesthetic appointments let things down somewhat, but the thing about looks is that they’re subjective – and the rest of the package far outstrips its price tag.

Alternatives

The regular D-X2E ($/£749) doesn’t have the wonderful neck of the Tuttle version, but it’s still a fine guitar for a lot less money. The other signature guitar in the X Series is the D-X2E Billy Strings ($949) and is another fine guitar that’s more ready to shred. Taylor’s Academy 10E ($799) is another quality Mexico-made dreadnought for not a lot of money.

The post Martin D-X2E Molly Tuttle review: “if I closed my eyes, I really could tell myself I was playing a 1940s guitar” appeared first on Guitar.com | All Things Guitar.
